chapter: Kid Rena, Kelly and the old trumpeters
title: Creole language and Rena's number 'Eh La Bas'
summary: His parents spoke Creole; Rena sang 'Eh La Bas' nightly, improvising words, and others also sang it.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: No, I don't talk Creole, not as much as I would like to. Of course my mother and father both speak very well.
Did they learn the regular French too?

Yes, they learned French, I guess it was handed down to them from their mothers and fathers. But I guess maybe one of the reasons why I didn't learn too much about it, because I was probably out in the streets someplace trying to see what's going on. And the only thing about it, I noticed when they used to have company and they were talking about something that they didn't want kids to know anything about, so they immediately went into Creole. So we were completely lost and we'd have to leave. So we were getting nothing out of the conversation anyhow. So I find it very fascinating and the thing that I liked about Rene, he used to do a number in Creole just about every night. And he used to bring the house down.
Do you remember what it was?
Well, the name, the number was He La Ba.
Yeah, he used to do that, He La Ba.
I noticed that Paul Barberin has got a recording on that in the stereophonic tape, which is very modern now. I would like to hear it. I've never heard it, but I've seen it advertised.
I haven't heard that particular tape. Yeah. Albert Burbank sings it. Well, Piku does too now. Oh yeah, yeah.

Well, those were the guys that used to sing it, like Piku and Kid Rene and some other fellas. Quite a few of them used to sing it because it was very popular. And a lot of times it was popular during the Mardi Gras too. Yeah, it was supposed to be a Mardi Gras.
Yeah. Were there any other Creole songs similar to that that they used, Rene or any of the others?
No, I don't think so. I don't remember too much about any other than that. But I remember it so much because at the time I was working with Rene, he used to do it just about once a night.
And he could sing it for a long time because he made words himself.

He made all the words himself. And of course from time to time there was always somebody in the audience that knew what he was talking about, knew what he was saying. And they in turn inspired the other people that didn't know what was going on to sort of get with the program as you might say.
